strengths: Proposes a novel and highly relevant paradigm shift from single-image perturbations to concept-based adversarial attacks, aligned with the capabilities of modern generative models.
Provides a solid probabilistic formulation (Theorem 1 & 2) indicating that expanding the distance distribution to concept-level reduces the divergence to the victim distribution.

Extensive evaluation metrics: The paper evaluates adversarial examples using a human user study, CLIP similarity, and seven distinct no-reference image quality metrics, demonstrating superior quality and semantic preservation.
Demonstrates excellent targeted attack success rates and strong black-box transferability, even against adversarially trained models.
Well-written, clearly illustrated (Figure 1 and 2), and provides detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters and additional surrogate models (MobileNet, ViT).
weaknesses: Extremely high computational cost: The method requires fine-tuning an SDXL LoRA (20 mins) and a diffusion model (8 hours) per concept on an H100 GPU, limiting its practicality in real-time or resource-constrained scenarios.

The theoretical analysis in Theorem 1 relies on the assumption of Gaussian distributions, which is a major simplification of complex neural network decision boundaries and high-dimensional image manifolds.

The dependency on an external complex pipeline (GPT-4o prompting, SDXL LoRA generation, and subsequent diffusion model training) makes the attack setup highly complex and sensitive to the quality of the generator and prompt models.
The comparison with ProbAttack ($|C_{ori}| = 1$) could more clearly dissect how much of the success is due to the concept-level formulation versus the powerful SDXL/GPT-4o data augmentation strategy.

strengths: Innovative conceptual contribution: The paper elegantly shifts the paradigm of unrestricted adversarial attacks from single-image perturbations to concept-level generation, offering a novel and mathematically sound way to define semantics-preserving attacks.

Rigorous probabilistic formulation: The authors provide a solid mathematical foundation by extending the probabilistic framework of adversarial attacks. Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, alongside the empirical estimation of KL divergence, provide clear theoretical support for why concept-level attacks outperform single-image attacks.

Strong and comprehensive evaluation: The empirical validation is thorough, showing significant improvements in targeted attack success rates and transferability across multiple surrogate architectures (ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base).

Thorough quality assessment: The evaluation of adversarial examples includes not only standard CLIP scores but also a crowdsourced user study and a suite of seven different no-reference image quality metrics, demonstrating that the generated images are both realistic and highly faithful to the target concept.

Effective concept augmentation pipeline: The integration of LLMs (GPT-4o) and diffusion models (SDXL LoRA) to augment a small set of images into a diverse, concept-preserving dataset is practical and well-designed.
weaknesses: High computational cost: The method requires extensive training time, specifically 20 minutes of LoRA finetuning and roughly 8 hours of diffusion model finetuning per concept. While acceptable for showing theoretical limits, this severely limits its real-time applicability.

Ambiguity in 'attack efficiency': The abstract claims 'higher attack efficiency', which might be interpreted by readers as faster computation. In reality, the method is computationally expensive, and 'efficiency' likely refers to sample efficiency or higher success rate per trial. The authors should clarify this wording.

Simplifying assumptions in Theorem 1: The theoretical proof of Theorem 1 relies on the assumption that the distance distributions are Gaussian with identical means. Since real-world image distributions on manifolds are highly non-Gaussian, the gap between this assumption and reality should be discussed.

Pipeline complexity and potential semantic drift: The framework relies on a multi-stage generative pipeline (GPT-4o -> SDXL -> DDPM). If the concept augmentation phase introduces semantic drift (e.g., generating incorrect variations of the concept), the subsequent adversarial distribution will also be flawed.

strengths: Addresses an interesting and relevant direction in unrestricted adversarial attacks by focusing on concept-level preservation rather than strict pixel-level distance constraints.
Proposes a practical engineering pipeline (integrating GPT-4o prompts and SDXL LoRA) to augment small, personalized image datasets to define a concept's distribution.

Provides a thorough empirical evaluation involving multiple surrogate models (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base), transferability to various architectures, and extensive image quality/user study metrics.
weaknesses: Unrealistic and Impractical Threat Model: The proposed attack requires training a personalized SDXL LoRA (taking 20 minutes) and fine-tuning a diffusion model (taking 8 hours) on a high-end NVIDIA H100 GPU for each individual concept. This massive computational footprint is completely impractical for real-world adversarial settings where attacks must typically be generated quickly.

Unfair Comparison with Baselines: The compared baseline methods (ACA, DiffAttack, ProbAttack) are only given a single reference image to generate the attack. In contrast, the proposed method utilizes 35+ images representing the concept (including generated variations). This discrepancy in information makes the performance comparison highly biased; baselines could perform significantly better or more robustly if allowed to leverage multiple views of the target concept.

Limited Algorithmic Novelty: The theoretical and probabilistic framework is heavily borrowed from ProbAttack (Zhang et al., 2024). The main extension is substituting a single-image distance distribution with a concept-level distance distribution. The actual technical contribution relies heavily on existing personalization tools (LoRA, DreamBooth) rather than a novel adversarial optimization technique.

Unrealistic Theoretical Assumptions: Theorem 1 assumes that the single-image distance distribution and the concept-based distance distribution are both Gaussian and share the exact same mean vector. In reality, a single image (a specific pose, background, and lighting) has a mean distribution that is highly shifted from a generalized concept distribution (which spans diverse backgrounds, viewpoints, and poses). Under different means, the analytical reduction of KL divergence does not necessarily hold.

Misleading Claims Regarding Efficiency: The abstract claims that the proposed framework achieves 'higher attack efficiency.' However, requiring 8 hours of GPU training per concept is the opposite of efficiency in comparison to traditional adversarial attacks that run in seconds or minutes. This claim is misleading without specifying that it might refer to a different notion of sample efficiency, while wall-clock efficiency is severely degraded.

strengths: Provides an interesting and novel extension of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework from a single image to a concept represented by a distribution.

Presents solid theoretical justification (Theorems 1 and 2) showing that expanding the dispersion of the distance distribution reduces the KL divergence to the victim distribution, which naturally translates to higher quality adversarial examples.
Exhibits highly competitive performance in targeted white-box attack success rates and transferability compared to state-of-the-art unrestricted attack baselines.
Conducts a comprehensive empirical evaluation of image quality and semantic preservation, supported by both a human user study and various advanced no-reference image quality metrics.
weaknesses: The computational cost is exceptionally high: the method requires approximately 8 hours of diffusion model fine-tuning per concept on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, which severely limits its scalability and real-world applicability.

The threat model assumes a strong scenario where the attacker must either possess a diverse set of images of the target concept or execute a complex pipeline (SDXL + LoRA + GPT-4o) to generate one, whereas typical attacks only require a single source image.

The absolute black-box targeted transfer success rates, although better than some baselines, remain relatively low (typically under 10% for targeted top-5 transfer), indicating limited viability for purely black-box red-teaming.

The overall attack quality is highly dependent on the generative model's ability to accurately capture and preserve the identity of the concept without introducing fine-tuning artifacts or identity drift.

strengths: Innovative and well-motivated concept: Shifting the paradigm from single-image perturbations to identity-level/concept-based adversarial attacks is a natural and highly relevant direction in the era of advanced generative models.

Solid theoretical foundation: The authors establish a principled probabilistic framework. Theorems 1 and 2 rigorously prove that expanding the attack from a single image to a concept (which increases dispersion) mathematically reduces the KL divergence between the distance distribution and the victim distribution.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper features extensive experiments across multiple surrogate architectures (ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, ViT, ConvNeXt) and tests transferability on a wide range of victim models, including adversarially robust ones.

Thorough quality assessment: The evaluation goes beyond attack success rates to include a robust human user study for concept preservation alongside seven different no-reference image quality metrics, demonstrating that the generated images are both natural and faithful to the original identity.

Excellent clarity and reproducibility: The paper is exceptionally well-written, provides clear intuitive figures, includes detailed proofs in the appendix, and commits to releasing the code and dataset.
weaknesses: High computational cost: The method requires significant compute, taking approximately 20 minutes for concept augmentation and 8 hours for diffusion model fine-tuning per concept. This represents a heavy bottleneck compared to online or optimization-only attacks like DiffAttack or ACA.

Heavy reliance on complex multi-stage pipelines: The framework depends on a combination of SDXL, LoRA, GPT-4o, and an additional DDPM-based diffusion model. This complexity makes the attack sensitive to the compounding errors or limitations of any single tool in the pipeline.

Limited black-box transferability under conservative settings: While white-box success is outstanding, targeted black-box transferability remains relatively low under the conservative (CONS) selection strategy, highlighting a distinct trade-off between concept preservation and cross-model transferability.

Conceptual overlap with existing guided-generation techniques: From an execution standpoint, the method closely resembles classifier-guided generation using a personalized/fine-tuned generative model (e.g., DreamBooth + classifier guidance). The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion positioning this against established guided generative sampling works.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting conceptual extension of the probabilistic framework of adversarial attacks (Zhang et al., 2024b) by shifting the focus from perturbing a single image to preserving a concept represented by a distribution.

The authors provide solid theoretical justification (Theorems 1 and 2) to show that expanding the distance distribution reduces the KL divergence from the victim distribution, facilitating targeted attacks.
The experimental evaluation is highly detailed, covering multiple surrogate and target architectures (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT, ConvNeXt), including adversarially trained defenses.
The proposed method generates high-quality images that preserve the identity of the concept very well, as supported by several no-reference image quality assessment (IQA) metrics and a user study.
weaknesses: Extremely high computational complexity: The method requires finetuning a Stable Diffusion LoRA model, generating augmented samples, and then finetuning a custom DDPM diffusion model for approximately 8 hours per concept on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. This makes the attack highly impractical for real-world scenarios compared to conventional adversarial attacks that take seconds or minutes.

Ambiguity of the threat model: Because the method generates entirely new images from scratch (varying backgrounds, poses, viewpoints) rather than modifying a specific input image, the boundary between an 'adversarial attack' and 'class-guided synthetic image generation' is blurred. Generating a new image of a corgi that looks like an ambulance is more of a study of out-of-distribution classifier vulnerability than a traditional adversarial evasion attack.

Low top-1 black-box transferability: While top-5 and top-100 metrics are reported, the top-1 targeted transfer success rates (Table Q.1) are extremely low (typically 1-2%). Given the massive computational budget (8 hours of training), one would expect more robust transferability.

The core methodology relies heavily on the framework of Zhang et al. (2024b), making the mathematical transition from a single image to a concept (replacing $x_{ori}$ with $C_{ori}$) somewhat incremental, with most of the novelty lying in the engineering pipeline (DreamBooth + LoRA + GPT-4o).
